summary: This RFC updates RFC 7296 by renaming IKEv2 Transform Type 5 from Extended Sequence Numbers to Sequence Numbers, and renames two values as well. It clarifies and extends the meaning of the transform type.

plainLanguage.summary: A label on a switch had a name that no longer fit everything it does. This renames it.

subtitle: IKEv2 Transform Type 5 stops being only about 'extended' sequence numbers and becomes a general way to describe IPsec sequence numbers.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 Transform Type 5 was named 'Extended Sequence Numbers (ESN)', which implies it can only negotiate whether ESN is used. That is too narrow for future needs such as agreeing that replay protection is not needed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC redefines Transform Type 5 as the properties of the sequence numbers of IPsec packets of an SA, renames it 'Sequence Numbers (SN)', and renames Transform IDs 0 and 1 to match what they already mean.
tldr.outcome: Only names and descriptions change. The bits on the wire and AH and ESP packet processing stay the same, and the door is open for new Transform IDs.

today: RFC 9827 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2025. It updates RFC 7296 and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC is a naming and clarification change to the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2). It updates RFC 7296 by renaming Transform Type 5 and the two Transform IDs defined for it.

IKEv2 is the usual way to set up IPsec Security Associations (SAs) for the Authentication Header (AH) and the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). During setup the peers negotiate parameters through transforms. The Transform Type says what is being negotiated, and each type has a list of Transform IDs that are the possible choices.
sections.plainLanguage: Two computers agree on the rules for talking securely before they start. This RFC fixes the name of one of those rules so the name matches what the rule really covers.

sections.title: Replay Protection in AH and ESP
sections.content:
IPsec offers an optional service called anti-replay. It works with a counter that only goes up, never wraps around, and is sent in the Sequence Number field of each AH or ESP packet. The receiver keeps a sliding window to spot duplicate packets.

The counter can be 32 bits or 64 bits. The 64-bit form is called Extended Sequence Numbers (ESN). Because the packet field is only 32 bits wide, with ESN the high-order 32 bits are not sent. The receiver works them out from packets it has already received.

The receiver alone decides whether to enable anti-replay, so a sender should always assume it is on. It should send increasing values and never let the counter wrap. The AH and ESP specifications allow a sender to skip keeping the counter only if it has been told anti-replay is disabled or cannot be achieved.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of numbered tickets at a deli counter. A number that has already been called is thrown away, so nobody can reuse an old ticket. Long numbers just mean the counter will not run out.

sections.title: The Problem with the Old Name
sections.content:
Transform Type 5 was named "Extended Sequence Numbers (ESN)" and had two values: "No Extended Sequence Numbers" and "Extended Sequence Numbers". IKEv2 therefore has no way to say that both peers agree replay protection is not needed. Even when both turn anti-replay off as receivers, each still has to keep increasing its sequence numbers as a sender.

There is also no way to tell receivers that replay protection is not possible for an SA, for example a multicast SA with several unsynchronized senders. Future IPsec protocols may also send full 64-bit sequence numbers or omit them from packets entirely, and those options would need to be negotiated.

Transform Type 5 is the natural place to do this, since it already negotiates how sequence numbers are handled. Its name, however, implies it only chooses whether to use ESN.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a menu item called 'Extra Large or Not'. If the cafe wants to offer a tiny size too, the name gets in the way. This RFC gives the menu item a name that allows more choices later.

sections.title: The New Meaning of Transform Type 5
sections.content:
The RFC redefines Transform Type 5 as the set of properties of the sequence numbers of IPsec packets of a given SA when those packets enter the network. It then clarifies the definition:

  • "Sequence numbers" may be logical entities such as counters built from information that is not sent on the wire, not only the content of the Sequence Number field.
  • The properties describe the packets of the SA, not the result of sender actions. With several unsynchronized senders, each may keep its own numbers unique, yet uniqueness across all packets is not guaranteed.
  • The properties apply to packets entering the network, not to what receivers get, because the network can break them (packet duplication breaks uniqueness).
  • The properties are read broadly, including the case where sequence numbers are absent.

Documents that define new Transform IDs should describe the properties of the sequence numbers and whether they allow replay protection. They should also say whether the new ID can be used with protocols that rely on particular properties, such as RFC 8750 (implicit IV in ESP) and RFC 9347 (aggregation and fragmentation for ESP). The RFC names G-IKEv2 (RFC 9838) as an example of a future Transform ID for multicast SAs.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule's name now says it is about how packets are numbered in general, including having no numbers at all. Anyone who invents a new numbering style has to explain what it does and does not guarantee.

sections.title: The Two Existing Transform IDs
sections.content:
The two existing values keep their meaning, and only get names that describe it.

Value 0 is renamed from "No Extended Sequence Numbers" to "32-bit Sequential Numbers". These are monotonically increasing 32-bit counters carried in the Sequence Number field of AH and ESP packets. They never wrap, are unique, and so suit replay protection and protocols that need uniqueness or monotonic increase.

Value 1 is renamed from "Extended Sequence Numbers" to "Partially Transmitted 64-bit Sequential Numbers". These are monotonically increasing 64-bit counters. The low-order 32 bits travel in the Sequence Number field and the receiver infers the high-order 32 bits. They also never wrap and are unique. To process incoming packets correctly, receivers must authenticate them, even when replay protection is not used.

Sender and receiver actions stay as defined in RFC 4302 for AH and RFC 4303 for ESP.
sections.plainLanguage: The two old settings are now called 'short counter' and 'long counter, only half shown'. They count the same way as before. Only the labels are clearer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it does not affect the security of the AH, ESP and IKEv2 protocols. It also notes that the descriptions do not change the existing semantics of the Transform IDs, that AH and ESP packet processing is unaffected, and that the bits on the wire do not change.
sections.plainLanguage: Because only the labels changed and nothing about how things work, nothing becomes more or less safe.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
IANA updated the registries in the IKEv2 Parameters group. In the "Transform Type Values" registry, Transform Type 5 is renamed to "Sequence Numbers (SN)", this RFC is added as a reference, and a note records the old name.

The registry "Transform Type 5 - Extended Sequence Numbers Transform IDs" is renamed "Transform Type 5 - Sequence Numbers Transform IDs". Transform IDs 0 and 1 get their new names, and notes record the old names. The range 2-65535, formerly "Reserved", is split. Numbers 2-1023 become Unassigned and 1024-65535 become Reserved for Private Use.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of names kept by IANA was updated with the new labels. It also keeps a note of the old labels so older documents still make sense.
